entries.claim: ID_TOKEN only matches a literal `id-token:` key, so `permissions: write-all` grants the job an OIDC id-token (write-all covers every scope, id-token included) and the guard does not flag it. That misses the stated goal of commit db1868e, failing any workflow that asks for an OIDC id-token.
entries.failure_scenario:
Change .github/workflows/test.yml line 8-9 to `permissions: write-all` (or put `permissions: write-all` on one job). Run on a scratch copy of the same regexes, workflowProblems returns [] for `permissions: write-all
jobs:
  j:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: echo hi
`. The suite passes, but the job can now mint an OIDC token and federate into Bedrock or Vertex, reaching a model with no key and no `secrets` mention. The flagged-cases table at line 72 tests only the literal `id-token: write` form.

entries.claim: The escape ban assumes \x, \u and \U are the only YAML escapes that matter, but a double-quoted YAML scalar also joins lines with an escaped line break (a trailing backslash, with the next line's leading whitespace stripped). A token split that way never appears whole in the raw text, so SECRETS, MODEL_KEY and EVAL all miss it and ESCAPE does not fire.
entries.failure_scenario:
A workflow with `env:
  CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN: "${{ secr\
     ets.MODEL_KEY }}"
  K: "ANTHROPIC_\
     API_KEY"
steps:
  - run: "claude plugin ev\
      al ."`. A scratch copy of workflowProblems returned [] for it. A YAML parser (PyYAML safe_load) resolves the same file to `${{ secrets.MODEL_KEY }}`, `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` and `claude plugin eval .`. Actions evaluates the `${{ }}` expression after YAML parsing, so the job gets a secret other than GITHUB_TOKEN, and the eval command, while the guard and its 'escaped model key' test (lines 48-56) pass. The same trick with an explicit key (`? "id-\
 token"
: write`) also parsed to `id-token: write` and the guard did not flag it, though I have not checked whether GitHub's parser accepts explicit keys.
